Reflection

Useful for triage, insufficient for proof

The central distinction: these records can show where reported vacancies are concentrated. They cannot show that a particular concept will succeed, why a unit is empty, or whether public support caused a change.

What the data supports

The September 2025 snapshot supports a consistent district comparison of reported storefront count, approximate vacancy duration, and reported floor area. The result is useful for selecting where staff should investigate first, shaping a small-space pilot, and monitoring whether the composition of vacancies changes in later snapshots.

Missing data

Earlier vacancy snapshots often omit floor area and vacancy year. The newest snapshot is much more complete, so the primary ranking uses that snapshot rather than pooling incompatible years. Boston coordinates also have some missingness; unmapped licenses are still retained in annual totals.

Bias and coverage

  • The Cambridge file is an administrative inventory, not a census of every available space. Reporting practice may change over time.
  • The Boston license file includes licensed food establishments only and only two source categories, FS and FT. It is not a complete competitor list.
  • Cottage-food records cover permitted operators. Informal, rejected, or never-submitted businesses are absent.
  • County Business Patterns can suppress detailed small-cell values and describe counties, not Cambridge commercial districts.

Uncertainty

Cambridge reports only a vacancy year, not a date. The analysis assumes July to estimate months, so individual durations can differ by roughly six months. District labels also change across historical snapshots; documented normalization improves comparability but cannot recover changes in the City’s underlying boundary definitions.

What this cannot prove

  • A high priority score does not mean public investment will produce a tenant.
  • Vacancy does not demonstrate unmet consumer demand or profitability.
  • License additions do not equal business openings, survival, or sales.
  • A cottage-food permit does not imply that its holder wants or can afford a storefront.
  • Observed relationships are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal.

Responsible next evidence

Before committing funds, the City should add rent and lease-term data, pedestrian counts, storefront accessibility, commercial-space condition, and an opt-in survey of merchants and property stakeholders. Those additions should be collected at an aggregate level and should not be published with personal identifiers.

Sources: all datasets listed on the Data page; accessed 2026-09-21. Units and definitions are documented in the methodology.

Descriptive evidence should guide investigation, not replace it.
